docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib is a reusable library of Invoke tasks shared across Python projects. Instead of copy-pasting the same tasks.py boilerplate (formatting, linting, type-checking, testing, environment setup, releasing, and documentation) into every repository, a project imports one namespace and gets a consistent set of invoke commands.

Quick Links:

  • Get Started
  • User Guide
  • Config
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Why invoke-tasklib?
docs.text:
Most Python projects end up with a tasks.py that wraps the same handful of tools: ruff, ty, pytest, docformatter, uv, mike. Keeping those wrappers in sync across many repositories is tedious, and small inconsistencies (a missing --xdoctest flag, a different coverage flag) creep in over time.

invoke-tasklib centralizes these tasks in one importable package:

from invoke_tasklib import make_ns

ns = make_ns()

invoke --list

A single invoke.yaml at the project root configures the package name and, optionally, the paths used by the tasks:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

See the user guide for the full config schema.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: We highly recommend installing invoke-tasklib in a virtual environment to avoid dependency conflicts.

docs.title: Prerequisite: uv
docs.text: Most tasks (env.*, release.* and security.audit) run uv, whichever way invoke-tasklib is installed. Install it first. A task that needs it and cannot find it stops with a hint that points to the same page.

docs.title: Using uv (recommended)
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package installer and resolver:

uv add --dev invoke-tasklib

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text:
Alternatively, you can use pip (uv is still needed to run the tasks listed above):

pip install invoke-tasklib

docs.title: Setting up a project
docs.text:
Starting from a typical project layout:

my_package/
├── src/
│   └── my_package/
│       └── __init__.py
├── tests/
│   └── unit/
├── pyproject.toml

docs.title: 1. Add a tasks.py
docs.text:
Add a tasks.py at the root of your project that imports the shared namespace:

# tasks.py
from invoke_tasklib import make_ns

ns = make_ns()

docs.title: 2. Add an invoke.yaml
docs.text:
Add an invoke.yaml at the root of your project with, at minimum, the package name:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

docs.text:
invoke format.check-python lint.check-python
invoke test.unit

If a task fails because a tool such as ruff or pytest isn't installed yet, run env.install first:

invoke env.install

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install invoke-tasklib from source, you can follow the steps below.

First, clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/invoke-tasklib.git
cd invoke-tasklib

Note: invoke-tasklib requires Python 3.11 or higher.

It is recommended to create a virtual environment (this step is optional):

uv venv --clear
source .venv/bin/activate

Then, install the project in editable mode along with its development dependencies:

uv sync --group dev

Finally, you can test the installation by running the unit tests:

python -m pytest tests/

docs.title: 'tasklib.package.name' must be set in invoke.yaml
docs.text:
Almost every task reads the config, which requires tasklib.package.name. An invalid config is reported with this one-line message and the exit code 2. Add an invoke.yaml at your project root (next to tasks.py) with at least:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

See Get Started and Config for the full schema.

docs.title: 'ruff' was not found on the PATH
docs.text:
Before running a command, the tasks check that its program (ruff, ty, uv, mike, ...) is on the PATH and exit with code 127 if it is not. Install the project tools with invoke env.install (the dev group has the linters and test tools, the docs group has mike) or activate the virtual environment that has them. Run invoke env.check-tools to list every missing tool at once; invoke check does the same for the steps it is going to run.

The hint depends on the program: uv and uvx point to the installation page of uv (env.install itself needs it), git, shellcheck and shfmt to the system package manager, and codespell to the project dependencies. The tools of the dev group (ruff, ty, pyright, docformatter, pre-commit, pytest and its plugins) and of the docs group (mkdocs, mike) name their group, for example uv sync --group docs.

Every command of a pipeline is checked. The NAME=value words before a program, the shell builtins (cd, export, test, [, exec, source, ., :) and the subshells and groups ((...), { ...; }, $(...)) are not looked up. Pass check=False to run to skip the check of a command. The module of python -m <module> is checked too (for example pytest), and is reported as The Python module 'pytest' is not installed for ... instead of Python's own No module named.

The pytest plugins of the options are checked as well: --xdoctest needs xdoctest, --timeout needs pytest-timeout, --cov* needs pytest-cov and --benchmark-only needs pytest-benchmark. A missing plugin is reported as The option --xdoctest needs the pytest plugin 'xdoctest' with the command that adds it, instead of pytest's unrecognized arguments.

docs.title: invoke: command not found after installing
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib depends on invoke, but installing a library into a virtual environment does not always put its console scripts on PATH the way you expect. Make sure:

  • Your virtual environment is activated (source .venv/bin/activate), or
  • You run it via uv run invoke ..., or
  • invoke itself is installed as a tool (uv tool install invoke). Note that env.create-venv installs the project, with invoke, into the new .venv, not as a tool.

docs.title: invoke --list shows no tasks / ns is empty
docs.text:
Check that tasks.py actually builds and exposes ns:

# tasks.py
from invoke_tasklib import make_ns

ns = make_ns()

Invoke discovers tasks from a module-level ns (or namespace) variable in tasks.py; if you renamed the variable or wrapped it, Invoke won't find it. (from invoke_tasklib import ns still works but is deprecated and warns.)

docs.title: A task fails with "command not found" (ruff, ty, shellcheck, ...)
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib tasks are wrappers around external CLI tools — it does not vendor them. Run invoke env.check-tools to see, in one list, which tools are available and which are missing. Install the missing tool, either directly or via your project's dependency groups:

invoke env.install                  # installs dev deps: ruff, ty, pytest, ...
invoke env.install --groups dev,docs  # additionally installs mike

shellcheck and shfmt are not Python packages; install them with your system package manager (e.g. brew install shellcheck shfmt on macOS) — see the Format page. The full external-tool matrix is in the User Guide overview.

docs.title: doc.publish-latest fails with No version tag found
docs.text:
doc.publish-latest reads the last git tag that looks like v1.2.3. Create a release tag (and fetch the tags in CI: git fetch --tags), or skip the tag lookup by passing the version:

invoke doc.publish-latest --version 1.2

docs.title: doc.publish-latest fails with Refusing to publish ... as latest
docs.text:
A newer version of the docs is already published, so publishing this one would move latest backwards. Pass --force if that is what you want.

See Doc.

docs.title: The output has [ok] and [fail] instead of emojis
docs.text:
On a terminal that cannot encode them (an ASCII locale, PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii), the progress messages use the tags [ok], [fail] and [skip] and leave the other emojis out. Use a UTF-8 locale (for example LANG=C.UTF-8) to get the emojis. Set INVOKE_TASKLIB_ASCII=1 to get the tags on any terminal, for example in a log that is read by a tool.

See Custom tasks.

docs.title: release.publish fails to authenticate
docs.text:
release.publish passes the PYPI_TOKEN (TEST_PYPI_TOKEN with --test-pypi, and UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN without it) environment variable to uv publish. Without a token it only works in GitHub Actions with the id-token: write permission (Trusted Publishing); anywhere else it stops with a clear message. Make sure the variable is set (e.g. as a CI secret) before running it:

export PYPI_TOKEN=pypi-...
invoke release.publish

export TEST_PYPI_TOKEN=pypi-...
invoke release.publish --test-pypi

See Release.

docs.title: fix-python / fix-docstrings / fix-shell changed files I didn't expect
docs.text:
fix_* tasks modify files in place by design (see the naming convention). Always run them on a clean working tree so the diff is easy to review:

git status   # make sure everything is committed first
invoke format.fix-python
git diff     # review what changed

docs.title: My custom paths aren't picked up
docs.text: Only paths.* keys you explicitly set in invoke.yaml are used; unset ones fall back to their default, which is derived from other keys, not from a previous override. For example, setting paths.tests also moves the default for paths.unit_tests (since it's derived from paths.tests), but setting paths.unit_tests alone does not affect paths.tests. See Config → Overriding Paths for a worked example.

docs.title: Where do I ask for help / report a bug?
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub. See the developer guide if you'd like to contribute a fix.

docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text: This document describes the internal architecture and design principles of invoke-tasklib.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
invoke-tasklib is designed around a simple idea: task modules are plain Invoke collections that share one config-resolution function. The core design follows these principles:

  1. One config entry point: every task reads project-specific values through invoke_tasklib.config.load_config (which wraps get_config and exits with a message on an invalid config), never directly from c.config.
  2. Convention over configuration: sensible defaults derived from package.name mean most projects only set one value (tasklib.package.name).
  3. Composability: make_ns() builds the default namespace; any subset of task modules can be imported and combined with project-specific tasks.
  4. No hidden state: tasks only run external commands (ruff, pytest, uv, mike, ...); they don't maintain state between invocations.

docs.title: 1. Config Resolution
docs.text:
invoke_tasklib.config.get_config(c) is the single source of truth for project-specific values. It:

  • Reads the tasklib key from the Invoke config (c.config), which Invoke itself populates from invoke.yaml.
  • Merges it on top of the defaults declared in SCHEMA (also exposed as DEFAULT_PACKAGE, DEFAULT_PATHS, DEFAULT_GROUPS, DEFAULT_TEST and DEFAULT_CHECK).
  • Rejects unknown keys and validates the values (package.python_version, package.import_name, groups.*, test.*, check.tasks).
  • Derives unset paths.* entries from package.import_name (for paths.src) or paths.tests (for the unit_tests/integration_tests/functional_tests/benchmarks entries).
  • Raises ValueError if package.name is missing, since nearly every task needs it, or if a value is invalid. Tasks call load_config, which turns the ValueError into an Exit.

Adding a key means adding one Option(default, validate, json_schema, doc) to SCHEMA and the field to the dataclass of its section (a test checks that they match), then one row in the uguide/config.md table (a test checks that too). The known keys, the defaults, the validation, the environment variable names and the JSON schema (python -m invoke_tasklib.config) follow from it.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TasklibConfig:
    package: PackageConfig
    paths: PathsConfig
    groups: GroupsConfig
    test: TestConfig
    check: CheckConfig

Returning frozen dataclasses rather than a raw dict gives task authors static typing on cfg.package.name and similar accesses, and the values cannot be modified by a task.

docs.title: 2. Task Modules
docs.text:
Each task module (formatting.py, lint.py, imports.py, typecheck.py, testing.py, env.py, release.py, doc.py, security.py, clean.py, check.py) is a collection of @task-decorated functions. clean.py and check.py also have a default task (clean.all, check.all) that is run by invoke clean and invoke check. A module groups tasks that operate on the same underlying tool or concern (e.g. most of testing.py wraps pytest, except test.doctest-markdown, which wraps the standard library's doctest module directly).

Tasks that need project-specific values call load_config(c) at the top of the function body; tasks that don't (e.g. lint.check_python) skip it entirely.

Three small modules support the task modules:

  • runner.py: run(c, command) is the only way a task runs an external command. It checks that the program is on the PATH (with a hint per program when it is not), echoes the command, and uses a pty only on a terminal. build_command builds a command line and quotes the arguments, and ARGS_HELP/PATHS_HELP are the help of the --args and --paths options.
  • output.py: say(c, message) prints a progress message (it never fails on a terminal that cannot encode the emojis) and the step context manager prints the start and done messages of a step, or a failure message.
  • _discover.py: lists the modules of a package without importing them. It is run in a subprocess by imports.check-isolated.

config.EXCLUDED_DIRS lists the directories that the tasks that walk the file tree (clean, format, test.doctest-markdown) never enter (.venv, .git, node_modules, ...).

docs.title: 3. The Namespace
docs.text:
invoke_tasklib/__init__.py has make_ns(*, exclude=(), include=None), which builds a new Collection by adding each task module (Collection.from_module(module, name=...)) as a sub-collection named after the module, leaving out the tasks of exclude and keeping only the tasks of include when it is set. The modules whose names would shadow the standard library or a builtin (format, types, test) are named formatting, typecheck and testing; the namespace names come from _MODULES, not from the module names.

This is what gives consuming projects format.check-python, test.unit, etc. via ns = make_ns() in their tasks.py, or a trimmed copy with make_ns(exclude=...). Each call returns a new collection, so a project can add its own tasks without affecting other importers. invoke_tasklib.ns, a collection built once and shared by every importer, is deprecated: accessing it emits a DeprecationWarning.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Here's how a task invocation flows through the system:

User runs `invoke test.unit --cov`
    ↓
Invoke loads invoke.yaml into c.config
    ↓
test.unit(c, cov=True) is called
    ↓
load_config(c) resolves package.name and paths.unit_tests
    ↓
Task builds the pytest command line with build_command (quoted)
    ↓
runner.run(c, cmd) checks the program, echoes the command and
executes it with c.run (pty only on a terminal)

docs.title: Why a Shared load_config Instead of Per-Task Config?
docs.text:
Rationale: A single resolution function keeps defaults and the validation of the config in one place, and guarantees every task sees the same resolved paths (e.g. test.unit and types.check agree on package.name).

Trade-off: Every task pays the (cheap) cost of re-resolving config on each call, rather than resolving it once. This is negligible since load_config does no I/O beyond reading c.config and, for the defaults that come from the project, two small files (.python-version and pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Why check_<target>/fix_<target> Naming?
docs.text:
Rationale: Makes the read-only/mutating counterpart of a task discoverable by name alone, and lets CI safely run every check_* task without risk of it modifying the working tree.

Trade-off: Slightly more verbose task names than a single format task with a --fix flag, but the split keeps invoke --list self-documenting.

docs.title: Why Frozen Dataclasses for Config?
docs.text:
Rationale: Static type checking (via ty) catches typos like cfg.path.src at development time, and attribute access reads better than nested keys, without requiring a runtime schema validation dependency.

Trade-off: The dataclasses don't validate values on construction; the validation is done by get_config (e.g. the package.name and package.python_version checks). It runs when a task starts, not when the collection is loaded, because the invoke.yaml values are only known once Invoke has built the context.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: Tests use invoke.context.MockContext, which records every c.run(...) call (made by runner.run) without executing it. This lets tests assert on the exact shell command a task would run, without depending on ruff, pytest, uv, etc. being installed or configured in the test environment. The unit tests also patch shutil.which (an autouse fixture in tests/unit/conftest.py) so that the check of the PATH done by invoke_tasklib.runner.run passes on any machine.

docs.title: Future Directions
docs.text:
Potential areas for enhancement:

  1. Additional task modules for other common project needs (e.g. changelog generation).
  2. A task to validate a project's invoke.yaml against the config schema ahead of time (the errors of get_config are only raised when a task runs).

cd invoke-tasklib

uv venv --clear
source .venv/bin/activate

.venv/bin/pytest tests -q

With coverage:

.venv/bin/pytest tests --cov=invoke_tasklib --cov-report=term-missing

Since invoke-tasklib itself uses invoke as its build tool, the project's own tasks.py (which composes tasks from invoke_tasklib) can also be used once the package is installed in editable mode - see the Makefile and invoke --list for the available tasks.

.venv/bin/ruff check src tests            # lint.check-python equivalent
.venv/bin/ty check

The doctests of the source and of the Markdown files are run with .venv/bin/inv test.doctest.

Or, once the package is installed:

invoke format.check-python
invoke lint.check-python
invoke types.check
invoke check          # the main checks in one command

docs.title: Adding a New Task
docs.text:
1. Pick the right module (formatting.py, lint.py, imports.py, typecheck.py, testing.py, env.py, release.py, doc.py, security.py, clean.py or check.py), or create a new one if the task doesn't fit an existing namespace.
  2. Follow the check_<target>/fix_<target> naming convention when applicable (see Format).
  3. Call load_config(c) if the task needs project-specific paths or the package name, rather than hardcoding them. Run the external commands with invoke_tasklib.runner.run and build them with build_command (it quotes the arguments), and print the progress with invoke_tasklib.output.say; do not call c.run or print in a task.
  4. Write a docstring (Google style) describing the task; its first line, one sentence, is the summary shown by invoke --list. Give each option a help entry in @task, and add --args (ARGS_HELP) and --paths (PATHS_HELP) when the tool accepts extra arguments or paths. The docstring is also used by the reference docs.
  5. Add unit tests using invoke.context.MockContext (see existing tests for the pattern).
  6. If the module is new, register it in src/invoke_tasklib/__init__.py (_MODULES and __all__).
  7. Update the README task table and the corresponding user guide page.

docs.title: Testing Guidelines
docs.text:
Tests use invoke.context.MockContext to capture the shell commands a task would run, without actually running them. Two helpers of tests/helpers.py are shared by the test modules: make_context builds a MockContext with an optional tasklib config, and commands returns the commands passed to c.run (run=True makes MockContext record the calls in a Mock). Import them instead of defining a copy in the test module:

from tests.helpers import commands, make_context

from invoke_tasklib import lint


def test_check_python() -> None:
    c = make_context({"package": {"name": "mypkg"}})

    *,
    keep_going: bool = False,

    skip: str | None = None,

Run the main checks of the project.

The steps are the ones of tasklib.check.tasks (by default format-python, format-docstrings, lint, types, imports and unit), run in that order. The other steps are doctest, shell, spelling, docs and audit. None of them modifies a file. By default the first failure stops the task; with keep_going every step is run and the failed ones are listed at the end.

Before any step is run, the tools that the selected steps need (PROGRAMS and MODULES) are looked up and all the missing ones are reported at once, with the code 127 and nothing run. With keep_going, only the steps that miss a tool are not run: they are reported as failed, with the missing tools as the reason.

get_config(c: Context) -> TasklibConfig

Return the effective tasklib config, merging user overrides from invoke.yaml (under the tasklib key) on top of the defaults.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default c Context

The invoke context.

required

Returns:

Type Description TasklibConfig

A frozen dataclass with the resolved package, paths,

TasklibConfig

groups, test, check and fix sections, each a

TasklibConfig

frozen dataclass too, e.g. cfg.paths.src.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If tasklib or one of its sections (package, paths, groups, test, check and fix) is not a mapping, or if tasklib or a section has an unknown key (for example a typo such as unit_test for unit_tests), or if tasklib.package.name is not set or is not a string, or if a tasklib.paths value is not a non-empty string, or if tasklib.package.python_version is not a string such as "3.10" (an unquoted 3.10 is read by YAML as the float 3.1), or if tasklib.package.import_name is not a Python module name, or if a tasklib.groups value is neither a string nor a list of strings, or if a tasklib.test value is invalid (a timeout and cov_fail_under must be integers, with a timeout > 0 and cov_fail_under between 0 and 100, cov_reports must be report formats, and xdoctest must be a boolean), or if tasklib.check.tasks or tasklib.fix.tasks is empty or has an unknown step.

Example usage:

>>> from invoke.config import Config
>>> from invoke.context import Context
>>> from invoke_tasklib.config import get_config
>>> overrides = {"tasklib": {"package": {"name": "mypkg"}}}
>>> c = Context(config=Config(overrides=overrides))
>>> cfg = get_config(c)
>>> cfg.package.import_name
'mypkg'
>>> cfg.paths.src
'src/mypkg'
>>> cfg.groups
GroupsConfig(install=('dev',), update=('dev', 'docs'))
>>> cfg.test.unit_timeout
10
>>> cfg.check.tasks[0]
'format-python'

all_(
    c: Context,
    *,
    keep_going: bool = False,
    only: str | None = None,
    skip: str | None = None,

Fix the lint and format issues of the project.

The steps are the ones of tasklib.fix.tasks (by default lint, format-python and format-docstrings), run in that order: the lint fixes come first, so that the formatting has the last word on the layout. The other step is shell. The steps modify files; check.all is the read-only counterpart. By default the first failure stops the task; with keep_going every step is run and the failed ones are listed at the end.

Before any step is run, the programs that the selected steps need (PROGRAMS) are looked up and all the missing ones are reported at once, with the code 127 and nothing run. With keep_going, only the steps that miss a tool are not run: they are reported as failed, with the missing tools as the reason.

Check that every module imports on its own.

Every module of the package (not only the subpackages) is discovered without being imported, then imported in its own interpreter. A module that fails to import on its own depends on something that is only initialized as a side effect of importing another module first, which is the usual symptom of a cyclic import. docs.text:
Reusable Invoke tasks shared across Python projects.

Typical usage in a consuming project's tasks.py::

from invoke_tasklib import make_ns

ns = make_ns()

and an invoke.yaml at the project root::

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

To compose a custom subset of tasks, use the exclude and include options of make_ns, or import individual task modules (the module of the test tasks is testing, so its collection needs the name test to keep the task names):

>>> from invoke.collection import Collection
>>> from invoke_tasklib import lint, testing
>>> ns = Collection(lint, Collection.from_module(testing, name="test"))
>>> sorted(ns.task_names)
['lint.check-python', 'lint.check-spelling', 'lint.fix-python',
 'lint.pre-commit', 'test.all', 'test.benchmark',
 'test.coverage-report', 'test.doctest', 'test.doctest-markdown',

say(c: Context, message: str, *, err: bool = False) -> None

Write a progress message followed by a newline.

The message goes to the output stream configured in the invoke context (run.out_stream), or to sys.stdout if none is configured. With err, it goes to run.err_stream or to sys.stderr instead, like the message of an Exit that invoke prints, so that a failure and its reason are on the same stream. Unlike logging, it needs no logging setup to be visible.

A message never fails a task: if the stream cannot encode a character (for example an emoji on an ASCII terminal), the status symbols are replaced by the tags [ok], [fail] and [skip] and the other emojis are removed. Set the environment variable INVOKE_TASKLIB_ASCII to 1 to get this ASCII output on any stream.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default c Context

The invoke context.

required message str

The message to write.

required err bool

If True, write to the error stream instead of the output stream.

False

Example usage:

>>> from invoke.config import Config
>>> from invoke.context import Context
>>> from invoke_tasklib.output import say
>>> say(Context(config=Config()), "hello")
hello

docs.title: Everyday Workflow
docs.text:
A typical local development loop looks like this:

invoke format.fix-python format.fix-docstrings   # auto-fix formatting
invoke lint.check-python imports.check-cycles types.check  # check quality
invoke test.unit --cov                            # run tests with coverage

To run the main read-only checks (format, lint, types, imports and the unit tests) in one command:

invoke check

See Check for the steps and the options.

And what CI typically runs (nothing should modify the working tree):

invoke format.check-python format.check-docstrings lint.check-python imports.check-cycles types.check
invoke test.all --cov

Since Invoke lets you chain multiple task names in one command, all of the above run as a single invoke call each.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to the Tools
docs.text:
Every task that runs an external tool takes --args, and the tasks that run on files also take --paths:

  • --args adds arguments to the command. The value is one string, split like a shell does.
  • --paths runs the tool on these files or directories instead of the default ones (the project for ruff, paths.src for docformatter and the source doctests, the scope directory for pytest, every *.sh file for shellcheck and shfmt, every markdown file for the markdown doctests).
Tasks --args goes to --paths test.all, test.unit, test.integration, test.functional, test.benchmark pytest ✅ test.doctest-src pytest ✅ test.doctest-markdown python -m doctest ✅ test.coverage-report coverage report ❌ format.*-python, lint.check-python, lint.fix-python ruff ✅ format.*-docstrings docformatter ✅ format.check-shell, format.fix-shell shellcheck, shfmt ✅ lint.check-spelling codespell ✅ lint.pre-commit pre-commit ❌ types.check ty (only) ✅ security.audit pip-audit ❌ doc.build, doc.serve mkdocs ❌ release.build uv build ❌ release.publish uv publish ❌

The tasks that have no option are the composite tasks (check.all, test.doctest), the tasks that run no external tool (clean.*, imports.*) and the tasks with their own options (env.*, doc.publish-*).

invoke test.unit --args "-k foo -x" --paths tests/unit/test_foo.py
invoke lint.check-python --args "--select E" --paths "src/a.py src/b.py"
invoke format.check-python --paths src/a.py
invoke security.audit --args "--ignore-vuln PYSEC-2024-1"
invoke doc.serve --args "--dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8001"
invoke test.coverage-report --args "--fail-under=90"

For types.check, --args goes to ty only and --paths goes to ty and pyright. The arguments and the paths are quoted, so they are never interpreted by the shell.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.check module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior check.all Runs the main read-only checks of the project (default)

check.all is the default task of the check namespace, so invoke check runs it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke check

Runs the steps of tasklib.check.tasks, in that order, and stops at the first failure. By default:

Step Task format-python format.check-python format-docstrings format.check-docstrings lint lint.check-python types types.check imports imports.check-cycles unit test.unit

Other steps can be added to the config (or run with --only): doctest (test.doctest), shell (format.check-shell), spelling (lint.check-spelling), docs (doc.build) and audit (security.audit). They are not in the default set because they need more tools (shellcheck, codespell, mkdocs) or the network.

tasklib:
  check:
    tasks: [format-python, lint, types, unit, doctest, docs]

None of them modifies a file.

Option Effect --keep-going Runs every step, prints the failed ones with the reason and exits with 1 if any failed --only Comma-separated steps to run instead of tasklib.check.tasks --skip Comma-separated steps to leave out 
invoke check --keep-going
invoke check --only lint,types
invoke check --skip unit

Before running anything, the task looks up the tools that the selected steps need and reports all the missing ones at once (exit code 127), so a missing ty is not discovered after the formatting has run. With --keep-going, only the steps that miss a tool are not run: they are reported as failed, with the missing tool as the reason. Run env.check-tools to see every tool of the tasks.

By default the task stops at the first failure, as the CI jobs do; use --keep-going locally to learn about all the problems in one run. Use the tasks directly (with --args and --paths) to run only one of them, or lint.pre-commit to run the hooks of the project. To leave check out of a collection, use make_ns(exclude=["check"]).

docs.title: Clean
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.clean module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior clean.all Removes build artifacts and caches from the repo root clean.pycache Removes all __pycache__ directories

clean.all is the default task of the clean namespace, so invoke clean runs it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke clean

Removes, if present, at the repository root:

  • Directories: build, dist, .pytest_cache, .ruff_cache, .coverage_html, htmlcov, .benchmarks, .mypy_cache, .tox, .nox, .hypothesis, and site only if the project has a mkdocs.yml or docs/mkdocs.yml file (what produces it)
  • Glob-matched directories: *.egg-info (at the root and in src) and every __pycache__ directory of the project. The .venv, .git, .pytest_cache and node_modules directories are never walked into, so nothing inside them is removed.
  • Files: .coverage, .coverage.* (parallel coverage data), coverage.xml

A top-level directory that contains files tracked by git (for example a build/ directory with scripts that are committed) is kept, and the task says so (⏭️ Keeping build: it contains files tracked by git). Outside a git repository, or without git, nothing counts as tracked. The caches (__pycache__, *.egg-info) and the files are not looked up.

Nothing is removed if the corresponding directory or file doesn't exist, so clean is safe to run repeatedly (it's idempotent) and doesn't fail on an already-clean checkout. A symbolic link to a directory is removed as a link, and the directory it points to is left untouched.

To see what would be removed without removing anything, add --dry-run (to clean.all or clean.pycache):

invoke clean --dry-run

It prints a Would remove <path> line per path instead of Removing <path>.

To remove only the __pycache__ directories:

invoke clean.pycache

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
This page describes the invoke_tasklib.config module, which resolves the shared config that all invoke-tasklib tasks read from.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python and Invoke.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every task in invoke-tasklib calls load_config(c) (get_config(c) with a clean exit on an invalid config, see below) to read project-specific values from an invoke.yaml at the root of the consuming project, under a tasklib key:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
    python_version: "3.14"
  paths:
    src: src/my_package
    tests: tests
    unit_tests: tests/unit
    integration_tests: tests/integration
    functional_tests: tests/functional
    benchmarks: tests/benchmarks
    docs_config: docs/mkdocs.yml
  groups:
    install: dev
    update: dev,docs
  test:
    unit_timeout: 10
    xdoctest: true
    cov_reports: html,xml,term
  check:
    tasks: format-python,format-docstrings,lint,types,imports,unit
  fix:
    tasks: lint,format-python,format-docstrings

Only tasklib.package.name (the distribution name, as on PyPI) is required. Everything else has a default, and most of the paths defaults are derived from package.name or from paths.tests.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Key Default package.name required package.import_name <package.name> with - replaced by _ package.python_version the .python-version file, else the requires-python lower bound, else "3.14" paths.src src/<package.import_name>, or <package.import_name> if only that directory exists paths.tests tests paths.unit_tests <paths.tests>/unit paths.integration_tests <paths.tests>/integration paths.functional_tests <paths.tests>/functional paths.benchmarks <paths.tests>/benchmarks paths.docs_config docs/mkdocs.yml groups.install dev groups.update dev,docs test.unit_timeout 10 test.integration_timeout 60 test.functional_timeout 60 test.xdoctest true test.cov_fail_under not set test.cov_reports html,xml,term check.tasks format-python,format-docstrings,lint,types,imports,unit fix.tasks lint,format-python,format-docstrings

The test section sets the per-test timeout in seconds of each test scope, whether pytest runs with --xdoctest (it requires the xdoctest package, so set xdoctest: false if the project does not have it; test.doctest-src ignores it and always uses the plugin), and a coverage threshold: with --cov, cov_fail_under is forwarded as --cov-fail-under. Timeouts and cov_fail_under are integers, xdoctest is a boolean. cov_reports is a comma-separated string or a list of the --cov-report formats of pytest-cov (html, xml, json, lcov, annotate, term, term-missing) that --cov generates. An empty value passes no --cov-report, so pytest-cov uses its default.

check.tasks is a comma-separated string or a list of the steps of check.all, run in that order: format-python, format-docstrings, lint, types, imports, unit, doctest, shell, spelling, docs and audit. It must have at least one step and no unknown step.

fix.tasks is the same for the steps of fix.all: lint, format-python, format-docstrings and shell, run in that order (the lint fixes first, so that the formatting has the last word on the layout).

package.import_name is the name used to import the package. It is used by imports.check-cycles, imports.check-isolated, release.build (the import check of the built artifacts) and the --cov option of the test tasks. Set it when it is not the distribution name with - replaced by _. It must be a Python module name.

If tasklib.package.name is missing, get_config raises a ValueError; the tasks use load_config, which turns it into an invoke.exceptions.Exit with the same message and the exit code 2 (no traceback).

Unknown keys in tasklib itself (typically a typo of a section such as path) and in the package, paths, groups or test sections (such as paths.unit_test) also raise a ValueError that lists the valid keys and suggests the closest one, instead of being silently ignored. Each section must be a mapping, package.name and every paths.* value must be a non-empty string, and test.cov_fail_under must be between 0 and 100.

package.python_version must be a quoted string such as "3.10" or "3.10.4". YAML reads an unquoted 3.10 as the number 3.1, so get_config raises a ValueError for any non-string or malformed value instead of silently creating a virtual environment with the wrong Python.

When the key is not set, the version is read from the project, in this order:

  1. the first line of the .python-version file, if it is a version such as 3.12 or 3.12.1 (an implementation name such as pypy3.10 is ignored);
  2. the lower bound of project.requires-python in pyproject.toml (">=3.11" gives 3.11);
  3. 3.14.

docs.title: Showing the Resolved Config
docs.text:
invoke config.show

Prints the tasklib section as the tasks see it, with every key and a comment with its origin. It answers "which value is used, and why" without reading the code:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: demo # project file
    import_name: demo # derived
  paths:
    src: lib # project file
    tests: zz # environment variable INVOKE_TASKLIB_PATHS_TESTS
    unit_tests: zz/unit # derived
    docs_config: docs/mkdocs.yml # default

The origin is the source with the highest priority that sets the key: default (the default of the library, or no value for an optional key), project file (invoke.yaml), environment variable INVOKE_TASKLIB_..., system config file, user config file, runtime config file or override (set from the command line or by code). derived is a value that no source sets, computed from other values or from the project (import_name, src, the test paths and the Python version). The config is validated first, so an invalid one stops the task with the usual one-line message. The task reads nothing but the config and the two project files of package.python_version, and changes nothing.

docs.title: Editor Completion (JSON Schema)
docs.text:
The keys, the defaults and the descriptions are declared once, in invoke_tasklib.config.SCHEMA (one Option per key: default, validation and JSON schema). The defaults, the key checks, the error messages and the JSON schema are all generated from it, so they cannot drift. Print the schema of the tasklib section of invoke.yaml with:

python -m invoke_tasklib.config > invoke-tasklib.schema.json

The same file is published with the documentation. Point your editor to it with a comment at the top of invoke.yaml to get completion and validation of the keys:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://durandtibo.github.io/invoke-tasklib/schema.json
tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

A test checks that the published docs/docs/schema.json equals the schema printed by the command (regenerate it with python -m invoke_tasklib.config > docs/docs/schema.json).

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Every key can also be set with an INVOKE_TASKLIB_<SECTION>_<KEY> environment variable, for example INVOKE_TASKLIB_PATHS_SRC=lib or INVOKE_TASKLIB_TEST_UNIT_TIMEOUT=30. This is handy in CI. It works because make_ns registers the defaults of the tasklib section with Invoke, which only reads the environment variables of the keys that it knows. The usual Invoke order applies: the environment variables win over invoke.yaml.

Invoke reads an environment variable as a string and converts it to the type of the default value: an integer for the timeouts, and, for a boolean such as INVOKE_TASKLIB_TEST_XDOCTEST, 0 or an empty value is false and anything else (including false) is true. test.cov_fail_under accepts a string of digits. A collection built by hand (Collection(lint, ...)) has no defaults, so it does not read the environment variables unless you call ns.configure({"tasklib": invoke_tasklib.config.default_config()}).

docs.title: Minimal Config
docs.text:
The smallest valid invoke.yaml only sets the package name:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package

With this, paths.src resolves to src/my_package, paths.unit_tests resolves to tests/unit, and so on.

docs.title: Overriding Paths
docs.text:
Override any individual path without affecting the others' defaults, for example when tests live outside tests/:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
  paths:
    tests: test
    benchmarks: test/perf

Here paths.unit_tests still resolves to <paths.tests>/unit, i.e. test/unit, since it is derived from the overridden paths.tests.

docs.title: Overriding Dependency Groups
docs.text:
env.install and env.update install uv dependency groups by name. Projects that define more groups than dev/docs (e.g. test, lint) can change the defaults those tasks use, instead of passing --groups on every invocation:

tasklib:
  package:
    name: my_package
  groups:
    install: dev,test
    update: dev,test,docs

Each value can also be written as a YAML list, which is joined with commas:

tasklib:
  groups:
    install: [dev, test]
    update: [dev, test, docs]

The --groups flag of the tasks stays a comma-separated string (--groups dev,docs).

docs.title: Using get_config in a Custom Task
docs.text:
get_config returns frozen dataclasses (cfg.package, cfg.paths, cfg.groups, cfg.test), so the values are read as attributes and cannot be modified. It raises a ValueError on an invalid config; use load_config in a task to exit with a message instead. get_config is the same function every built-in task uses, so a project-specific task can read the same config:

from invoke.tasks import task
from invoke_tasklib.config import get_config


@task
def my_task(c):
    cfg = get_config(c)
    print(cfg.package.name, cfg.paths.src)

docs.title: Writing a Custom Task
docs.text: This page shows how to write a task of your own that behaves like the tasks of invoke-tasklib. The helpers below are the supported public API for that: their signatures are documented in the reference pages (runner, output and config).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Helper Use it to invoke_tasklib.config.load_config Read the resolved config; an invalid one exits cleanly invoke_tasklib.runner.build_command Build a command line with quoted arguments and paths invoke_tasklib.runner.run Run a command: echo, pty only on a terminal, program check invoke_tasklib.runner.check_program Check that the programs of a command are installed invoke_tasklib.output.say Print a progress message invoke_tasklib.output.step Print the start and the end of a step, and ❌ Failed: ... on error

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# tasks.py
from invoke.tasks import task

from invoke_tasklib import make_ns
from invoke_tasklib.config import load_config
from invoke_tasklib.output import step
from invoke_tasklib.runner import ARGS_HELP, PATHS_HELP, build_command, run


@task(help={"args": ARGS_HELP, "paths": PATHS_HELP})
def check_complexity(c, args=None, paths=None):
    r"""Check the complexity of the code with radon."""
    cfg = load_config(c)
    with step(c, "🔍 Checking the complexity...", "✅ Complexity check passed"):
        run(c, build_command("radon cc", args=args, paths=paths, default_paths=[cfg.paths.src]))


ns = make_ns()
ns.add_task(check_complexity)
  • Read the config with load_config(c), not from c.config: it merges the defaults, validates the values and exits with a one-line message on an invalid config. The tasklib section is available as cfg.package, cfg.paths, cfg.groups, cfg.test and cfg.check.
  • Build the command with build_command: the program is used as it is, and the user's args and paths (and the default paths) are split like a shell does and quoted, so a space or a ; never splits or injects a command.
  • Run it with run: it echoes the command, uses a pty only on a terminal, and first checks that the program is on the PATH (with an installation hint if it is not). Do not call c.run directly. For python -m <module>, the module is checked only when the command uses the running interpreter (python_executable(), the one that runs invoke): for another interpreter or a python found on the PATH, a missing module is reported by Python itself (No module named ...), without a hint. Use python_executable() in your commands.
  • Report the step with step: it prints the start message, then the done message, or ❌ Failed: <what was being done> on the error stream (stderr, like the message of an Exit) if the block raises (the exception is raised again, so the exit code is unchanged). Use say for any other message (say(c, msg, err=True) writes to stderr); neither fails on a terminal that cannot encode an emoji: ✅, ❌ and ⏭️ become [ok], [fail] and [skip], and the other emojis are removed. Set INVOKE_TASKLIB_ASCII=1 to get this output on any terminal.

Follow the naming convention of the shared tasks: check_<target> never modifies a file and fix_<target> does. Add the task to a make_ns() result, as above, so it does not leak into other importers.

>>> from invoke_tasklib.runner import build_command
>>> build_command("radon cc", args="-s", paths="a.py 'my dir'", default_paths=["src"])
"radon cc -s a.py 'my dir'"

docs.title: Adding a Shortcut for an Existing Task
docs.text:
add_task with a name registers a task of the library under one more name, at the top level of the collection. The task keeps its own name in its namespace:

>>> from invoke_tasklib import make_ns
>>> from invoke_tasklib.release import build
>>> ns = make_ns()
>>> ns.add_task(build, name="build-package")
>>> "build-package" in ns.task_names
True
>>> "release.build" in ns.task_names
True

The tasks.py of this repository does it for release.build: inv build-package is the command that the composite action durandtibo/build-pypi-package-action runs, as the release workflow shows. Such a shortcut shows up in invoke --list of the project, so add one only for a name that something else (a CI action, a script) depends on.

docs.title: Testing a Custom Task
docs.text:
invoke.context.MockContext records the commands without running them:

>>> from invoke.config import Config
>>> from invoke.context import MockContext
>>> from invoke_tasklib.runner import run
>>> c = MockContext(config=Config(), run=True)
>>> _ = run(c, "ls")
>>> c.run.call_args.args[0]
'ls'

docs.title: Doc
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.doc module, which provides tasks to publish versioned documentation with mike, on top of MkDocs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior doc.build Builds the docs, failing on warnings doc.serve Serves the docs locally doc.publish-dev Publishes development (unstable) docs doc.publish-latest Publishes latest (stable) docs

All four tasks read paths.docs_config from the resolved config (default: docs/mkdocs.yml). The two publish tasks pass it to mike via --config-file, and doc.build and doc.serve pass it to mkdocs.

docs.title: Publishing Development Docs
docs.text:
invoke doc.publish-dev

Deploys the current docs under the main version with the dev alias (mike deploy replaces an existing main version, so it is not deleted first), then pushes to the configured remote (typically gh-pages). Pass --no-push to only commit the docs branch locally.

docs.title: Publishing Latest (Stable) Docs
docs.text:
invoke doc.publish-latest

Determines the version to publish from the highest git release tag (a tag like v1.2.3, read with git tag --list 'v[0-9]*'; pre-release tags such as v1.2.0rc1 are ignored), truncated to <major>.<minor> (e.g. 1.2). It then deploys the current docs under that tag with the latest alias, and sets latest as the default version shown to visitors. Pass --no-push to only commit the docs branch locally.

To publish a specific version without looking at the git tags, pass it explicitly:

invoke doc.publish-latest --version 1.2

The task fails if there is no version tag and no --version, because publishing under a made-up version would be a setup error. Pre-release versions (1.2.0rc1, 1.2.0a1, 1.2.0.dev1, ...) are skipped, so they never become latest.

The task also refuses to move latest backwards: if a newer <major>.<minor> is already published (mike list --json), for example when releasing a 1.1.5 backport after 1.2.0, it fails with Refusing to publish 1.1 as latest. Pass --force to publish the older version anyway.

docs.title: Local Preview
docs.text:
The publishing tasks are meant for CI (they --push to the remote). To check and preview docs locally:

invoke doc.build
invoke doc.serve

doc.build runs mkdocs build --strict, so a broken link or a missing reference fails the task (unlike a mike deploy into a throw-away branch, which does not). doc.serve runs mkdocs serve with live reload. Both use paths.docs_config and need the docs dependency group.

doc.build and doc.serve take --args for mkdocs, for example invoke doc.serve --args "--dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8001".

docs.title: Env
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.env module, which provides tasks to set up and inspect a project's Python environment using uv.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior env.create-venv Creates a virtual environment and installs the project env.install Installs project dependencies and the package (editable) env.update Updates dependencies and pre-commit hooks env.check-tools Checks which tools of the tasks are available env.show-installed-packages Shows the installed packages env.show-python-config Shows the Python configuration

docs.title: Creating a Virtual Environment
docs.text:
invoke env.create-venv

Creates (or recreates) a .venv using the package.python_version from the resolved config (by default the version of .python-version or the lower bound of requires-python), and then runs env.install (uv sync --locked), so the environment has invoke within the bounds of the project and the packages that tasks.py imports, such as invoke-tasklib. The task is run with invoke, so invoke must already be available (for example through uv tool install invoke) to run it. It accepts no option: use env.install to choose the dependency groups.

Warning

This clears any existing .venv.

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text:
invoke env.install

Runs uv sync --locked, which also installs the package itself in editable mode. --locked fails if uv.lock is out of date with pyproject.toml instead of silently using it (run uv lock to refresh it).

Flag Default Adds to uv sync --optional-deps on --all-extras --groups groups.install (default dev) --group <name> for each comma-separated group

--groups takes a comma-separated list of dependency groups to install, e.g. dev,docs. A group listed twice is installed once. Pass an empty string to skip installing any group.

Disable the on-by-default optional deps, or override the groups, with:

invoke env.install --no-optional-deps --groups ""
invoke env.install --groups dev,docs

The default value of --groups comes from the resolved config's groups.install ("dev" unless overridden in invoke.yaml), so a project with more groups than dev/docs can change the default once instead of passing --groups on every call.

docs.title: Updating Dependencies
docs.text:
invoke env.update

Runs uv lock --upgrade, updates the pre-commit hooks (pre-commit autoupdate, only if the project has a .pre-commit-config.yaml file), and reinstalls the project with the groups from --groups (default: the resolved config's groups.update, "dev,docs" unless overridden).

invoke env.update --groups dev,docs,test

Warning

Updating dependencies may introduce breaking changes. Review the changes and run the test suite afterward.

docs.title: Inspecting the Environment
docs.text:
invoke env.show-installed-packages
invoke env.show-python-config

env.show-python-config prints the installed Python versions known to uv, the interpreter uv would select, and the interpreter currently on PATH. It does not fail when no python is on the PATH.

docs.title: Checking the Tools
docs.text:
invoke env.check-tools

env.check-tools gives a single view of the tools that the tasks run: the programs (uv, uvx, git, ruff, ty, pyright, docformatter, codespell, pre-commit, shellcheck, shfmt, mkdocs, mike) and the Python modules of the interpreter (pytest, coverage, xdoctest, pytest_timeout, pytest_cov). Each tool has one line, with its path when it is available:

✅ ruff: /project/.venv/bin/ruff
❌ shfmt: program not found. Install shfmt with your system package manager, ...

All the tools are listed, so one run shows everything that is missing. The task does not read the config, so it can be run before invoke.yaml is set up. It exits with the code 127 if a tool is missing, so it can also gate a CI job. It does not install anything: see env.install.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.fix module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior fix.all Fixes the lint and format issues (modifies files)

fix.all is the default task of the fix namespace, so invoke fix runs it. It is the counterpart of check.all, which never modifies a file.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke fix

The steps are the ones of tasklib.fix.tasks (see Config), by default:

  1. lint: lint.fix-python (ruff check --fix);
  2. format-python: format.fix-python (ruff format);
  3. format-docstrings: format.fix-docstrings (docformatter).

The other step is shell (format.fix-shell, shfmt). The order matters: the lint fixes run before the formatting, which has the last word on the layout, so a second run changes nothing.

Option Effect --only Comma-separated steps to run instead of tasklib.fix.tasks --skip Comma-separated steps to leave out --keep-going Runs every step and lists the failed ones, instead of stopping

Like check.all, the programs of the selected steps are looked up before anything runs, and all the missing ones are reported at once with the exit code 127. With --keep-going, only the steps that miss a tool are not run; they are reported as failed.

Warning

The steps modify files in place. Commit your work before running them.

docs.title: Format
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.formatting module, which provides tasks for checking and fixing code, docstring, and shell script formatting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tasks follow a check_<target> / fix_<target> naming convention:

  • check_<target> tasks are read-only: they fail with a non-zero exit code if formatting is wrong, but never modify files.
  • fix_<target> tasks modify files in place to match the expected format.
Task Behavior format.check-python Checks Python formatting with ruff (read-only) format.fix-python Formats Python code with ruff (in place) format.check-docstrings Checks docstring formatting with docformatter (read-only) format.fix-docstrings Formats docstrings with docformatter (in place) format.check-shell Checks shell scripts with shellcheck (read-only) format.fix-shell Formats shell scripts with shfmt (in place)

docs.title: Checking Format
docs.text:
invoke format.check-python
invoke format.check-docstrings
invoke format.check-shell

These are safe to run anywhere, including in CI, since they never modify files.

docs.title: Fixing Format
docs.text:
invoke format.fix-python
invoke format.fix-docstrings
invoke format.fix-shell

Warning

fix_* tasks modify files in place. Ensure your work is committed before running them.

docs.title: Docstring Style
docs.text: format.check-docstrings and format.fix-docstrings run docformatter against paths.src from the resolved config, using the [tool.docformatter] section of the consuming project's pyproject.toml (via --config ./pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Shell Scripts
docs.text:
format.check-shell and format.fix-shell operate on every *.sh file in the project. The .git, .venv, .pytest_cache, node_modules, build, dist and site directories are not searched, so third-party scripts (for example the activation scripts of a virtual environment) are never checked or rewritten.

Note

shellcheck and shfmt are not Python packages, so they aren't installed by env.install. Install them with your system package manager, e.g. brew install shellcheck shfmt on macOS or apt install shellcheck on Debian/Ubuntu (shfmt there comes from the golang-go toolchain or a release binary).

format.check-shell and format.fix-shell take --args for the tool and --paths to run on given scripts instead of every *.sh file of the project.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.imports module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior imports.check-cycles Checks for import cycles with a static import graph, and prints them (read-only) imports.check-isolated Checks that every module imports on its own, one interpreter per module (read-only)

docs.title: Checking for cycles
docs.text:
invoke imports.check-cycles

The import graph of package.import_name (from the resolved config) is built from the source files with ast: nothing is imported, so the result is deterministic, does not depend on the order of the imports, and needs no subprocess. import a.b is an edge to a.b, from a import b is an edge to a.b if it is a module (else to a), and relative imports are resolved. Imports of other packages are not edges. The strongly connected components of the graph are the cycles; each one is printed as a path and the task exits with 1:

Found 1 import cycle(s) in mypkg:
  mypkg.a -> mypkg.b -> mypkg.a

An import that does not run when a module is imported cannot cause a cycle, so by default the imports under if TYPE_CHECKING: and the imports inside functions are ignored:

Option Effect --lazy Also follows the imports inside functions --type-checking Also follows the imports under if TYPE_CHECKING:

A syntax error is reported as such (with the module). So is a relative import that goes above the top-level package (from .. import x in pkg/a.py), which Python rejects too. A missing optional dependency is not reported at all, because neither is a cycle.

docs.title: Checking that every module imports on its own
docs.text:
invoke imports.check-isolated

This is the former behavior of imports.check-cycles. It discovers every module of the package (__main__ modules are skipped) without importing anything, then imports each one in its own python -c process with the interpreter that runs Invoke. A module that fails to import on its own depends on something that is only initialized as a side effect of importing another module first, which is often the symptom of a cycle. It also fails on a missing dependency or a syntax error, and it starts one interpreter per module, so it is slow for a package with heavy imports (and the traceback of the subprocess is shown as it is).

docs.title: Lint
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.lint module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior lint.check-python Checks code linting with ruff (read-only) lint.fix-python Fixes auto-fixable linting issues in place with ruff lint.check-spelling Checks the spelling with codespell (read-only) lint.pre-commit Runs all the pre-commit hooks on all the files

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke lint.check-python

This runs ruff check .. In GitHub Actions (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true) it adds --output-format=github, so ruff annotates violations directly on the diff; locally the readable default output is used. Pass --output-format to choose the format explicitly:

invoke lint.check-python --output-format=concise

invoke lint.fix-python

This runs ruff check --fix ., which rewrites files in place for every auto-fixable violation. Not every lint rule is auto-fixable, so lint.check-python may still report violations afterwards that need a manual fix.

Warning

lint.fix-python modifies files in place. Commit your work before running it.

docs.title: Spelling and Pre-commit Hooks
docs.text:
invoke lint.check-spelling

This runs codespell . (the configuration is read from pyproject.toml). --args and --paths work as for the other tasks.

invoke lint.pre-commit

This runs pre-commit run --all-files. Pass --args to select a hook, e.g. --args ruff-format. The hooks may modify files.

docs.title: Release
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.release module, which provides tasks to build and publish the package to PyPI using uv.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
release.pypi was renamed to release.publish; the old name is no longer available.

Task Behavior release.build Builds the package and verifies installation (--check also validates metadata with twine) release.publish Checks the git state, then builds and publishes the package to PyPI or TestPyPI

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
invoke release.build

Runs uv build, then verifies the artifacts it produced: the newest wheel and the newest source distribution in dist/ are each installed in an isolated uv run environment (uv run --isolated --no-project --with dist/<file>) and the package is imported from it. The task fails if the build did not produce a wheel or a source distribution.

Pass --check to additionally validate the package's PyPI metadata with twine check:

invoke release.build --check

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI
docs.text:
invoke release.publish

Before anything is built, the task checks the git state: the working tree must be clean, HEAD must be tagged and the tag (without a leading v) must be the static project.version of pyproject.toml (a dynamic version is not compared). It then asks for a confirmation, unless --yes is given or the CI environment variable is set to something other than 0 and false. Finally it builds the package (via release.build, which clears dist/ first so stale artifacts are never uploaded) and runs uv publish.

Credentials, in this order:

  • a token in PYPI_TOKEN (TEST_PYPI_TOKEN with --test-pypi, because the two indexes reject each other's tokens and a PyPI token must not be sent to TestPyPI) or, without --test-pypi, in UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN (usually the production token, so it is never used for TestPyPI), handed to uv publish through its environment so it never appears on the command line;
  • PyPI Trusted Publishing (OpenID Connect), used automatically in GitHub Actions with the id-token: write permission (--trusted-publishing always); no token is needed.

Without either, the task fails before building.

Option Effect --test-pypi Publishes to TestPyPI instead of PyPI --dry-run Runs the checks and the build, and gives --dry-run to uv publish; no token --yes Does not ask for a confirmation --skip-checks Does not check the git state --args Extra arguments for uv publish 
invoke release.publish --dry-run
invoke release.publish --test-pypi --yes

Warning

This publishes a new version to PyPI, which cannot be undone. Try --dry-run or --test-pypi first, and make sure you are releasing the intended version.

release.build takes --args for uv build.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.security module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior security.audit Audits the locked dependencies for known vulnerabilities (read-only)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke security.audit

This exports uv.lock to a temporary requirements file (uv export --locked) and audits it with uvx pip-audit against known vulnerability databases (via PyPI's Advisory Database). It exits non-zero if the lock file is out of date or if a vulnerability is found.

The task does not sync or modify the environment, and the result depends on the lock file, not on what was installed last. pip-audit does not have to be a dependency of the project.

Use --args to pass options to pip-audit, for example to accept an advisory:

invoke security.audit --args "--ignore-vuln PYSEC-2024-1"

docs.title: Test
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.testing module, which provides tasks to run doctests, unit/integration/functional tests, and benchmarks with pytest.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Behavior test.doctest Runs doctests on source code and markdown files test.doctest-src Runs doctests on source code test.doctest-markdown Runs doctests on Python examples in markdown files test.unit Runs unit tests test.integration Runs integration tests test.functional Runs functional tests test.all Runs all tests (unit, integration, and functional) test.coverage-report Generates an HTML/terminal report from existing coverage data test.benchmark Runs performance benchmarks

All test tasks (except test.benchmark, test.doctest, and test.doctest-markdown) run pytest with --xdoctest enabled, so doctests embedded in the code under test are also collected. Set tasklib.test.xdoctest: false if the project does not have the xdoctest package.

docs.title: Running Doctests
docs.text:
invoke test.doctest

Runs both test.doctest-src and test.doctest-markdown.

invoke test.doctest-src

Runs doctests against paths.src from the resolved config. It always runs pytest --xdoctest: tasklib.test.xdoctest only applies to the test scopes, since the task has no purpose without the plugin. If the xdoctest package is missing, the task stops with a message that names it; use test.doctest-markdown alone in a project that does not have the package.

invoke test.doctest-markdown

Recursively finds every *.md file in the project (skipping .venv, .pytest_cache, .git, and node_modules) and runs, for each one:

python -m doctest -o NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE -o ELLIPSIS -o REPORT_NDIFF <file>.md

so Python code examples embedded in markdown files (README, docs, ...) stay correct and up to date. NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE and ELLIPSIS make output comparisons more forgiving (whitespace differences are ignored, and ... in expected output matches any text), and REPORT_NDIFF gives a readable diff when an example's output doesn't match. A markdown file with no >>> doctest blocks is still visited but simply reports zero tests, so it always "passes". The task reports the number of files it checks: the files of --paths when it is set, otherwise every markdown file of the project.

docs.title: Running Tests by Scope
docs.text:
invoke test.unit
invoke test.integration
invoke test.functional

Each targets its own path (paths.unit_tests, paths.integration_tests, paths.functional_tests), with a longer default timeout (60s vs 10s) for integration and functional tests, since they typically exercise more of the system. The timeouts are the test.unit_timeout, test.integration_timeout and test.functional_timeout values of the config. If the directory of test.integration or test.functional does not exist, the task prints a message and skips it instead of failing with a pytest error. test.unit does the same, except that when paths.unit_tests does not exist but paths.tests does (a flat tests/ layout), it runs the whole paths.tests directory.

invoke test.all

Runs everything in paths.tests in a single pytest invocation, with the largest of the three timeouts (60s by default, since the integration and functional tests are part of that directory).

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Pass --cov to test.unit, test.integration, test.functional, or test.all to generate coverage reports. The formats are the test.cov_reports value of the config (html,xml,term by default, each one is a --cov-report of pytest-cov; an empty value leaves the choice to pytest-cov):

invoke test.unit --cov

test.integration --cov and test.functional --cov append to any existing coverage data (--cov-append), so they compose with a prior test.unit --cov run to build up combined coverage across scopes:

invoke test.unit --cov
invoke test.integration --cov
invoke test.functional --cov

If tasklib.test.cov_fail_under is set, it is passed as --cov-fail-under and the task fails when the coverage is lower. Since the integration and functional tasks append to the existing data, run test.unit --cov first (it replaces the data) or coverage erase, otherwise the result depends on what was run before.

invoke test.coverage-report

Runs python -m coverage (the interpreter of the tests) to regenerate the HTML report and prints the terminal summary from whatever coverage data (.coverage) is currently on disk — the data produced by an earlier --cov run — without re-running the tests. Pass --open-browser to also open htmlcov/index.html in your default browser:

invoke test.coverage-report --open-browser

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
invoke test.benchmark

Runs pytest --benchmark-only against paths.benchmarks. This requires pytest-benchmark to be installed. The task is skipped with a message if paths.benchmarks does not exist.

test.benchmark, test.doctest-src and test.doctest-markdown take --args and --paths, and test.coverage-report takes --args (for example --fail-under=90).

docs.title: Types
docs.text: This page describes the invoke_tasklib.typecheck module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Task Behavior types.check Checks type hints with ty (read-only)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
invoke types.check

This runs ty check.

Pass --complete to also run pyright after ty (slower, more thorough):

invoke types.check --complete

--args is passed to ty only, and --pyright-args to pyright only (it is used with --complete); --paths is passed to both tools (see Passing Arguments to the Tools):

invoke types.check --complete --args "--python-version 3.12" --pyright-args "--pythonversion 3.12"

Without --paths, ty checks the project and pyright the files of its own include setting (in pyproject.toml or pyrightconfig.json), so the two tools can look at different files. Set the same files in both, or pass --paths, to keep them aligned.
